deep.reconstruction:
CONTEXT. This page belongs to the 'Litt. H' sequence (fol. 62-64). It works out the method of Theoria Motus (1809) for determining an orbit from three geocentric observations, applied to a concrete example. The previous page set up the example: α, α', α'' are the geocentric longitudes, β (log tan) the latitudes, V, V', V'' the Earth's heliocentric longitudes, and R, R', R'' the Sun-Earth distances (logs 9.9946906, 9.9935938, 9.9932002). That page also obtained a linear relation of the form δ = A − B/r³ for a curtate geocentric distance δ. This page has three parts: (I) a general recipe for eliminating r from that relation; (II) the numerical solution of the resulting equation for the middle observation under the 'Erste Hypothese'; (III) recovery of δ and δ'' from δ'.

I. GENERAL RECIPE.
Notation for one observation:
- b is the geocentric latitude; V−α is the elongation in longitude.
- p is defined by cos p = cos b·cos(V−α) (the elongation from the anti-solar direction, i.e. the angle at the Earth measured from Sun→Earth produced).
- ω is the angle of the right spherical triangle with legs b and V−α and hypotenuse p. Hence tan b = sin(V−α)·tan ω and sin b = sin p·sin ω, so R cos b sin b/sin ω = R cos b sin p.
- φ is the angle at the planet in the plane triangle Sun-Earth-planet.

Geometric relations. With ρ = δ/cos b the true geocentric distance, the sine rule gives:
- r = R sin p / sin φ;
- ρ = R sin(φ−p)/sin φ, hence δ = R cos b·sin(φ−p)/sin φ = R cos b (cos p − sin p·cot φ).
In the old notation this is δ = R cos²b cos(V−α) − R cos b sin b/(sin ω·tan φ) = R cos²b {cos(V−α) − sin(V−α)/(cos ω·tan φ)}. [My step: sin b/sin ω = cos b·sin(V−α)/cos ω.] Likewise r = R sin b/(sin ω sin φ) = R cos b sin(V−α)/(cos ω sin φ).

Elimination of r [my filling of the implicit algebra]:
1. Substitute the geometric expressions into δ = A − B/r³: R cos b (cos p − sin p cot φ) = A − B sin³φ/(R³ sin³p).
2. Multiply by sin φ: (A − R cos b cos p) sin φ + R cos b sin p cos φ = B sin⁴φ/(R³ sin³p).
3. Put tan H = R cos b sin p/(A − R cos b cos p) [= R cos b sin b/(sin ω{A − R cos²b cos(V−α)})]. The left side becomes R cos b sin p·sin(φ+H)/sin H.
4. Hence sin(φ+H) = sin⁴φ · B sin H/(R⁴ cos b sin⁴p) = sin⁴φ · B sin⁴ω sin H/(R⁴ sin⁴b cos b).

This is Gauss's one-unknown transcendental equation (TM art. 141: c·sin⁴z = sin(z ± ζ)). Once φ is found, δ and r follow from the formulas above.

Second variant ('Oder wenn'): δ = a cos b − b cos b/r³, i.e. ρ = a − b/r³. Then:
- tan H = R sin p/(a − R cos p);
- sin(φ+H) = sin⁴φ · b sin H/(R⁴ sin⁴p);
- δ = R cos b sin(φ−p)/sin φ;
- r = R sin p/sin φ.
(The letter b is reused for a constant.)

II. NUMERICS, middle observation, Erste Hypothese (k = k°, μ = M = 1).
Input values:
- log tan β' = 9.4952246;
- log sin(V'−α') = 9.9166769n;
- log cos(V'−α') = 9.7516745n, where V'−α' = 235°37'53.29";
- log cos β' = 9.9797335.

Computation of p: log cos p = 9.7314080n and log sin p = 9.9255437n give p = 237°23'58.79". Also log R' cos β' = 9.9733273 and log R' sin p = 9.9191375.

Coefficients: log Σ = 8.3984242 is carried over. A block of Gaussian-logarithm work gives log a = 9.6774833 and log b = 9.6570965.

Angle H: a scaled quantity with log 9.6798995 is combined with |cos p| by Gaussian addition (0.2760389 = log(1 + ·/|cos p|); 0.2760389 + 9.7314080 = 0.0074469). Then log tan H = log sin p − 0.0074469 = 9.9180968n. A first value H = 249°7'4.67" is struck out; the adopted value is H = 140°22'15.37".

Coefficient c of the equation:
- log sin H = 9.8046946;
- log b + log sin H = 9.4617911;
- 4·log(R' sin p) = 9.6765500;
- so log c = 9.7852410, where sin(φ+H) = c·sin⁴φ.

Root: φ = 238°5'56.70". Results:
- log sin φ = 9.9288889;
- log r' = 9.9191375 − 9.9288889 = 9.9902486;
- log sin(φ−p) = 8.0866043, with φ−p = 0°41'57.91";
- log δ' = 9.9733273 + 8.0866043 − 9.9288889 = 8.1310427n.
A side computation (9.9797335, 8.1231731, 0.0708215) yields 8.1737281, labelled log δ', which is used further on.

Correction factor: 8.1485392 is the log of a half-product of reduced time intervals. Subtracting 3·log r' = 9.9707458 (an earlier 9.9698770 is also used) and taking log(1 + x) gives the factor 1 + τ τ''/(2 r'³) for the ratio of triangle areas, written 0.0064942. The next page uses 0.0064912.

III. FIRST AND THIRD DISTANCES.
Inputs combined: sin(V−α) = 9.6484176n, sin(V''−α'') = 9.9996562n, the ratios β/θ, sin(V''−V') etc. (log sin(V'−V) = 9.3890511), and the correction factor. From these Gauss forms linear relations of the type {0.2393817·δ'' + 1} = {0.5346262·δ'' + 1}·0.0011341 (logs). He solves by Gaussian logarithms with repeated trial values:
- δ'': log δ'' = 7.9194764, then 7.7834960n;
- δ: log δ = 8.5356615, then 8.4735682n.

Final values ('Daraus'): log δ = 8.4735682n, log δ' = 8.1310427n, log δ'' = 7.7834960n. The next page uses them to get heliocentric places, r, r'' and the second hypothesis.

The distances are tiny (|δ'| ≈ 0.0135) and negative. φ−p is small and r' ≈ R', so the root found lies near the trivial 'Earth' root of the sin⁴ equation; whether this was intended or the example is a test cannot be decided from this page.
errors: The transcribed r = R sin b/(sin ω cos φ) and R cos b sin(V−α)/(cos ω tan φ) cannot be right: the sine rule requires r = R sin b/(sin ω sin φ) = R cos b sin(V−α)/(cos ω sin φ) = R sin p/sin φ. This is either a misreading or a slip in the first two members; the final member R sin p/sin φ is correct and is the one used.
In the middle line for δ, the factor read as 'tan ψ' should not be there (it looks struck out). The correct expression is R cos²b sin(V−α)/(tan φ cos ω).

The correction-factor log written 0.0064942 does not match its inputs. From 8.1786622 one gets log(1.0150891) = 0.0065042, which also appears at the bottom as 0065041. With 3 log r = 9.9707458 one gets 0.0064913, the value used on the next page. 0.0064942 is probably a digit slip (~1e-5 in the log), and it propagates into the δ, δ'' work of this hypothesis.
Two different values are both labelled log δ' (8.1310427n from the sine formula, and 8.1737281). The second is used in the δ, δ'' equations; its derivation is unclear and may be a different quantity.
A first value H = 249°7'4.67" was struck out and replaced by 140°22'15.37", which satisfies log tan H = 9.9180968n with the correct quadrant. This is a self-correction, not an error.
Log a = 9.6774833 versus 9.6798995 used for tan H: the small difference (0.0024162) is unexplained, possibly a scaling (e.g. by R or cos b) or an intermediate correction.

results.what: Elimination of r between δ = A − B/r³ and the Sun-Earth-planet triangle via the auxiliary angle H, giving the single equation sin(φ+H) = sin⁴φ·B sin H/(R⁴ cos b sin⁴p), plus δ = R cos b sin(φ−p)/sin φ and r = R sin p/sin φ
results.modern_name: Gauss's equation of the eighth degree in Gauss's method of preliminary orbit determination (sin(z−ω) = m sin⁴z form)
results.usually_credited_to: C. F. Gauss, Theoria Motus (1809), arts. 140-142 (worked out c. 1801-1806)

results.what: Area-ratio approximation n/n'' ≈ (τ/τ'')(1 + τ τ''/(2 r'³)), applied as a log correction factor
results.modern_name: Gauss's (and Lagrange's) series approximation of triangle/sector ratios in the three-observation method

results.what: Recovery of the first and third curtate distances from the middle one via the coplanarity linear relations, solved iteratively with Gaussian logarithms
results.modern_name: Gauss's method of successive hypotheses (Erste/Zweite Hypothese) for preliminary orbits

results.what: Conversion of geocentric ecliptic coordinates to the elongation angle p via cos p = cos b cos(V−α), sin b = sin p sin ω

deep.surprise_reason: This is a worked draft of the orbit-determination procedure Gauss published in Theoria Motus (1809): the auxiliary angle, the sin⁴ equation, and successive hypotheses. It is well documented as his and dates from his own 1801-1806 work. The only interest is as a working document showing his numerical practice (Gaussian logarithms, trial roots, self-corrections).

'μ = 1' corresponds to 'M = 1' on the previous page; 'k = k°' is the hypothesis on the ratio of the k's.
